name: Bloodletting for leanness

card.summary: A historical practice of drawing blood for health and bodily balance, revived in some fringe circles in the hope of a leaner, cleaner look.
card.note: Documented harms of bloodletting include infection, anaemia and hypovolaemic shock.

quick.overview:
Bloodletting is the removal of blood for health purposes, one of the oldest medical practices, drawn from humoral theory in which health depended on the balance of four bodily fluids. Fringe circles have revived the idea for body composition, with the hope of looking leaner or having a cleaner physique.

Modern medicine uses supervised therapeutic phlebotomy for specific conditions such as hemochromatosis and polycythemia. No published trials have tested it as a way to lose fat or look leaner.
quick.how: Historically it involved cutting a vein or using leeches or cupping. Modern clinical phlebotomy is done by trained staff in healthcare settings, and blood donation is the everyday form. This article does not describe do-it-yourself methods.
quick.risks: Documented harms include significant blood loss, infection, hematoma, anaemia and hypovolaemic shock. Self-performed bloodletting carries the same risks without clinical supervision.

lead: Bloodletting was among the most common medical practices from antiquity to the late nineteenth century, carried out in ancient Egypt and Greece and through medieval Islamic, Talmudic and Ayurvedic medicine. Under humoral theory, practitioners believed illness came from an imbalance of blood, phlegm, black bile and yellow bile, with excess blood ('plethora') treated by removal [1].

In a looksmaxxing context the practice is discussed as a way to become leaner or to improve the body, in line with older ideas of purifying or balancing the body. These claims come from fringe circles and are not part of modern clinical practice.

Today therapeutic phlebotomy is a standard treatment for hemochromatosis and also used for polycythemia, porphyria cutanea tarda and some other conditions, performed by trained staff [1]. Studies of related practices such as acupoint bloodletting concern conditions like stroke recovery, not body composition [2].

angle.text: Practitioners of the revived idea hope that removing blood will leave them leaner or healthier-looking. No trial has tested bloodletting for fat loss or appearance.

paras: Galen held that blood was the dominant humour and laid out detailed rules for how much to draw based on age, season and location. Printed surgical manuals in the 1500s helped standardise the practice [1].

William Harvey's work in 1628 on circulation undermined its theoretical basis. In the 1830s Pierre Louis used statistical methods to show that phlebotomy did not help in pneumonia and fevers. Use declined through the nineteenth century, although a 1923 textbook edition still recommended it [1].

Therapeutic phlebotomy is the mainstay treatment for hemochromatosis and is used in polycythemia, porphyria cutanea tarda and some other conditions [1]. Leeches are still used in some surgical and other settings [1][3]. Traditional East Asian medicine also uses acupoint bloodletting, and a 2024 meta-analysis assessed it for acute stroke recovery [2].
Documented harms of bloodletting include significant blood loss, infection and sepsis, hematoma, anaemia and fatal hypovolaemic shock [1].

No studies found on bloodletting for leanness or body composition. Clinical research on related practices addresses other conditions, such as a 2024 systematic review of bloodletting for acute stroke recovery [2].
